institutionName: University of Natural Resources and Life Sciences, Vienna (BOKU)

questions.question: What motivated you to go on exchange? (pick the most important one) *
questions.answer: Explore new cultures

questions.question: Please explain: *
Which aspects were crucial to choosing your study destination? *
questions.answer: I first of all wanted to go somewhere, I could take some interested courses, and BOKU has an extensive and very interesting course catalogue. Besides that I was very keen on going to a destination that wasn't too bleak and sad during autumn and winter. I love the Austrian Christmas markets, and there's a great "wine hiking" season in Vienna as well, so I think it's a great destination for the A/W semester, also good opportunities for hiking and skiing of course. I also really wanted to go traveling while on exchange, and I got to discover a lot of neighbouring cities and countries from Vienna. Lastly I was happy to improve my German as well

questions.question: How would you rate your overall study abroad experience? *
Additional comments:
questions.answer: I had a fantastic exchange semester, I definitely recommend Austria, Vienna and BOKU as an amazing exchange destination! The academic level of the courses is somewhat lower than at KU and it was a kinda stressful having to take so many small courses at the same time.

questions.question: How easy was it to find the information you needed to know upon arrival? *
questions.answer: In my experience the information was good. There was a zoom meeting for all incoming exchange students in May, we received a lot of e-mails with check lists and we had 5 intro days before the semester start, which was really great (also for the social aspect). I had the feeling that both the BOKU administration and the Buddy students were very available to help. The only thing that was difficult in terms of information is that you can't plan your courses and schedule before you physically register at BOKU.

questions.question: What assistance, if any, did you receive when you arrived at your study destination? *
questions.answer: E-mails, presentation at intro week, briefing when I registered at the university, I also had a Buddy assigned who I could ask questions.

questions.question: Overall, how satisfied were you with the orientation and assistance available to students at your host institution upon arrival? *
Additional comments
How did you find housing? *
questions.answer: I found housing on my own

questions.question: Did you live on campus or off campus? *
questions.answer: Off campus

questions.question: What options were available for on campus housing? *
What options were available for meal plans or cooking facilities? *
What should future exchange students know about living in on campus housing? *
How easy was it to find off campus housing? Any recommendations? *
questions.answer: There is a lot of housing available in Vienna! Both dorms and shared apartments (in German: WG), the quality and price vary a lot though. BOKU has a lot of dorms recommended on their website, which you can check out. I used the app/website WG-Gesucht to find a WG, where I got a room from another girl who was going on exchange at the same time, so I had her room and shared the flat with one house mate. I started looking at the end of July and there was still quite a lot of options, but more expensive.. If you can I recommend to start looking in May/June maybe.

questions.question: What should future exchange students know about living off campus? *
questions.answer: It's good.. There's not really options to live on campus

questions.question: Overall, how satisfied were you with the housing available to students? *
Additional comments:
How easy did you find the registration process at your host institution? *
Additional comments:
questions.answer: Registering at the university is pretty straight forward, however you do need to show up in person on campus to register, and only after that can you register for courses. The course registration process is more tricky. It's a lot of work to get the schedule to add up without overlaps in courses, and since you can only start this proces after you have arrived at in Vienna, some of the courses you might've wanted could be full.

questions.question: Please describe the registration process at your host institution *
questions.answer: You make an appointment to go to the Türkenschanz campus to register, you get your BOKU card with your Matrikelnummer and then you can make a profile on the website BOKUonline. On BOKUonline you register for courses and can see your schedule, exam dates, grades etc..

questions.question: What kind of help was available? *
questions.answer: There was good help both from the administration like from the Internation Relations office and also from other students and the "buddies". The Studo app is really useful, where you can see previous students' review of the courses, the Erasmus WhatsApp groups are great, and genereally if you e-mail the IR-office or the professors, they are all very helpful and nice, in my experience.

questions.question: How successful were you in registering for the classes you wanted? *
questions.answer: I was pretty succesful! Think there was 1-2 courses I wanted that I didn't get, but it wasn't really a problem, since the course catalogue at BOKU is so extensive that you have loads to choose from. It also helped me that I arrived already a month before the semester start, so I could get the spots before others. I signed up to maybe 30 courses to try them out and then scaled down and ended up with 10 courses of 30 ECTS total I quite liked after a month or so of deciding.

questions.question: What advice would you offer to future exchange students about registration at your host institution? *
questions.answer: If you can arrive early to do you registration etc,  I would say do it. Generally it's also advised to sign up to all the courses you find interesting at the start, so you make sure you get a spot, and then you can start seeing how they all fit together in your schedule. The first two weeks of the semester a lot of students try out many different courses and thereafter make their decision. If you don't get into a course, sign up to the waitlist anyways, and also maybe email the professor and you can even show up to the first lecture to ask for a spot. This worked for me. Also use the Studo app to see the reviews of the different courses by other students, it's super super useful!

questions.question: How satisfied were you with the academic programme at your host institution? *
Additional comments:
questions.answer: I had some interesting courses, and I think BOKU has a great variety in the academic programme with a good focus on sustainability. I however wasn't the biggest fan of the low amounts of ECTS per course (usually only 2-3 ECTS), since it's kinda messy to have to juggle 10 different courses at the same time and the courses generally lack depth.

questions.question: Were you a BA or MA student at UCPH when you were on exchange? *
questions.answer: BA

questions.question: Did you take BA or MA classes while you were on exchange *
questions.answer: Both

questions.question: Please elaborate on the level of courses *
questions.answer: I would say the level is generally lower than at KU. I was doing my 5. semester on my bachelor and had mainly masters courses, and I didn't find them very challenging. From my own experiences and what I've heard, the courses at campus Muthgasse (biotech, water technology, green chemistry, food science etc.) are more difficult than the ones taught at main campus Türkenschanz (natural resources, biology, nature management etc.). Also the final exams are often just paper and pen, so not with any notes or books available like a lot of exams at KU are. Sometimes you get the possible exam questions before to prepare, or you can find old ones on Studo, so it's more just about memorising the curriculum.

questions.question: How did the style of teaching at your host institution compare with that of UCPH? *
questions.answer: At KU the courses are generally bigger like 7.5 ECTS and therefore also contain more styles of teaching within one course; a course can have both lecture, exercises, excursion, project and/or lab work all in one. The style of teaching at BOKU depends a lot on the course, where the teaching style is defined by codes such as VO, VS, VU, VX, EX etc., where V means lecture, S means seminar, U means exercises, X means excursions and so on. So that means unless you choose a specific course for it, you might not have any lab or group work at all in the whole semester. Also, there are no books, so you save that money and generally don't have to read for the classes, unless you have a course where it is part of the student assesment and clearly defined before. This is very different from KU, where you have to read loads, so it was a pretty nice break, but it also means you need to go to the lectures to learn stuff.

questions.question: How long were you on exchange? *
questions.answer: 1 semester

questions.question: Please list the courses you were enrolled in during your first semester. *
questions.answer: Aquaculture in practice - lectures and field trips. Biobased and biodegradable plastics. Conservation biology. Development research and practice. Ecology of aquatic systems. Environmental toxicology (in German: Umwelttoxikologie). Field camp I - introduction to mountain forestry and forest sciences. German for Science (BOKU specific topics) - Course A (B2+). Intensive German Refresher Course - moderate advanced. Organisational behaviour.

questions.question: Please list the courses you were enrolled in during your second semester. *
What specific courses would you recommend to future exchange students? Why? *
questions.answer: My top recommendation is the Field camp I! It's six days excursion in a cabin in the lower alps with a group of 20 ish mountain forestry students - really cosy, super interesting and not a difficult course to follow. I also very much recommend the German courses, especially the intensive German before the semester starts, which is a chance to make friends early and check off 3 ECTS before the semester even begins. Aquaculture in practice was about fish production in lakes and consisted of four field trips and only two lectures, so it was super easy. Conservation biology (the master course, not the bachelor!!) was relaxed and pretty interesting. Develppment research and practice and Organisational behaviour were both interesting, had 10 minute tests at the start of each lecture and no final exam - they were the only courses I had with mandatory classes and reading material.

What unexpected costs did you encounter? *
questions.answer: My Danish phone bill got really expensive after 4 months abroad, so then I chose/had to get extra data with an Austrian sim card through Airalo. I also wasn't aware of the fee when you register your address at the municipality/"Magistrat" - apparently if you use another ID than your passport it is a lot cheaper.

questions.question: What items were more or less expensive than you expected? *
questions.answer: I think I expected the general prices to close to as cheap as they are in Germany, but a lot of the time it was similar prices to Denmark. Groceries are pretty much as expensive as in Denmark. Fun things like going out to eat or to the cinema and stuff like that are generally cheaper though. Wine and beer is quite cheap, shots and cocktails not cheap. The food at the uni canteen is not cheap, but the döner shop at uni is a very good alternative.

questions.question: How satisfied were you with the non-academic opportunities (clubs, sports, etc.) at your host institution? *
Additional comments:
questions.answer: All was great, there are sooo many options! BOKU and the social Erasmus organisation ESN do a lot of work to offer so many events and different things to be a part of or experience.

questions.question: What kinds of cultural, athletic and social activities were available for students at your host institution? *
questions.answer: There were lots of social activities; such as the whole intro week, the weekly international table, the "Stammtisch", creative Tuesday and lots of other events organised by BOKU, the student bar "Tüwi" and by the ESN. The BOKU Ball was the biggest highlight! You can join different well-priced sports through the USI (like the KSI at KU), and BOKU has an american football team and basket ball team, the BOKU Beez, that play against other university teams.

questions.question: Which non -academic activities would you recommend to future exchange students? Why? *
questions.answer: The BOKU Ball! It was so much fun and a cool experience being at a traditional ball at the Rathaus. Participate in the Stammtisch and the events and trips planned by the ESN. Check out the 7., 8. and 9. district for great coffee shops, bars and thrift stores! Go traveling and experience more of Austria and the neighbouring countries.

questions.question: What do you recommend other visiting students see or do on their weekends or holidays? *
questions.answer: Go traveling! If you get the Jugend Vorteilskarte (25 years or younger) you can get 50% discount on all train tickets within Austria. I think the card costs around 20 euros, so it's definitely worth it if you do a couple trips. Within Austria I went to Salzburg and on a cabin trip somewhere two hours from Vienna and also on a few hiking trips. I also did a daytrip to Bratislava and weekendtrips to Prague, Brno and Budapest.

questions.question: How easy was it to adjust to the local culture of your exchange site? *
questions.answer: It was fairly easy for me personally, since the Austrian and Danish culture isn't too dissimilar. I also have lived in Copenhagen for a few years and in Berlin for two years, and I would say Vienna is kind of like a good mix between those two cities.

questions.question: Do you have any tips for socializing with local students?
questions.answer: Attend courses with excursions or group work, or sign up to sports classes through USI or attend some of the other events at BOKU like creative Tuesdays, salsa dancing etc.

questions.question: What, if any, cultural differences did you find particularly challenging? *
questions.answer: I didn't find the cultural differences too challenging, it's not so dissimilar from the Danish culture. I think I just sometimes felt Vienna was a bit crowded with people and traffic compared to Copenhagen, but it's still quite clean and safe and nothing compared to other big cities, so not something big to complain about haha. I missed being able to cycle on my bike everywhere easily and the ocean.

questions.question: What parts of the culture did you most appreciate? *
questions.answer: I thought it was really cool to experience a country with a culture that has been shaped by both western, eastern and southern European influence. The Austrian history and society has many layers and I didn't know as much about it before I came as I do now. It was fun to experience the fancier Viennese culture like the balls, the opera and the coffee houses. The mountains, the wine hills and all the nature around also really influence the culture, I really enjoyed hiking and especially the "wine hikes" in the 19. district.

questions.question: What are the three most important things you would tell a UCPH student who is going to your host institution on exchange? *
questions.answer: 1) Get to Vienna 2-4 weeks early to register on site so you can start registering for courses and maybe even do an intensive German course, which is well worth it. My first month before semester start I also already made a lot of friends through different Erasmus WhatsApp groups and got to know the city better! 2) Try to find accomodation in the sweet spot between BOKU and the city or somewhere with good public transport. Some cool districts are 7., 8. and 9., I lived in the 17. district by Alser Straße station on the U6, and that was great for both getting to campus quick and out in town. 3) Try to take courses that don't all have a final exam in the last semester week, it will make it a lot less stressful - some have exams earlier, some have mandatory attendance at lectures and then no final exam and some have a paper or a presentation instead. Also look into doing courses with field trips/excursions included or courses that don't run for the full semester. If you prioritise a bit of time to work out your courses and your schedule, you can make your life a lot easier and the semester much more enjoyable!

questions.question: Is there any other information that you think might prove useful to future exchange students attending your host institution? *
questions.answer: Download the Studo app to see your schedule easy and to check other students' reviews of the courses and get their old exam papers. Download the Wienmobil app for transport tickets within Vienna and the ÖBB app for tickets in the rest of Austria and to the airport. Get the ESN card to go to their parties and on their trips, it also gives you good discounts on Flixbus and Ryanair and other stuff.

questions.question: What was the most rewarding part of your exchange experience? *
questions.answer: Meeting all the amazing people I did, traveling around that part of Europe and having a semester where I had to figure everything out for myself. I had time to reflect a lot on what I like to do with my free time, what kind of people I like to surround myself with and what actually interests me academically. I was also happy with how much my German improved in the time I was there and now I know a bunch of Austrian slang that I may never use again in my life, but it's cool!

questions.question: What was the greatest challenge during the exchange? *
questions.answer: Even though I had a roommate and spent time with people nearly every day, I did feel quite lonely sometimes. It can be difficult to not have your go-to people around you if you want to do something, but also don't have the social energy to meet with people you don't know very well yet. It could also be really hard to prioritise your time and energy sometimes, since there always seems to be plans you can partake in, but you also need to rest and study once in a while. The Erasmus FOMO is real, and you need to learn to listen to yourself and your own needs

questions.question: Any other comments?
questions.answer: It might seem like a lot right now, but I promise all the work is worth it once you are on your exchange! I had a lot going on in my life when I applied and I also doubted at times if it was the right thing to go, but I am so happy I did it in the end. Remember to listen to yourself and take time to figure out what makes you happy and prioritise doing those things. Your exchange might not go exactly how you pictured in your head, or you might not find "your people" in the first week (my best friends from exchange was people I only started talking more to in my last two months there), and you might not get the courses you want, but it's still all gonna work itself out! Viel Erfolg, bussi baba!

questions.question: Do you agree to share your travel report with other fellow students? *
questions.answer: Yes
